Identity & Access Management

One binary for SSO, MFA, and OpenID Connect.

IAM Server gives your apps single sign-on, multi-factor authentication, and standards-based OpenID Connect. It adds CAS support and protects other apps behind a reverse proxy. You need only the binary and a PostgreSQL database.

Get started API reference Deploy to production

OIDC & OAuth 2.0

Act as an authorization server for your apps, with PKCE, discovery, and JWKS.

CAS 2.0 / 3.0

Serve older apps that speak CAS. Bridge them to modern SSO providers.

MFA & passkeys

Enforce TOTP, WebAuthn/FIDO2, and single-use backup codes.

Reverse-proxy auth

Protect any app behind Caddy or Traefik with a forward-auth endpoint.

00 Introduction

What IAM Server is

IAM Server is a self-hosted identity server. It ships as one Go binary with the admin UI built in.

The server does five jobs:

  • It acts as an OIDC / OAuth 2.0 provider for your apps.
  • It acts as a CAS server for older apps.
  • It lets users sign in with Google, GitHub, or any OIDC provider (Microsoft, Okta, GitLab, or Keycloak).
  • It enforces MFA (authenticator apps and passkeys).
  • It protects other apps behind Caddy or Traefik with forward-auth.

This page is a static reference. It describes the server in general. It does not read this instance's live configuration.

01 Installation

Install & run

Choose one path. Use local development to work on the code. Use production to run the server for real.

Requirements

GoVersion 1.26 or later. It builds the server.
NodeVersion 22 or later. It builds the web UI only.
DockerIt runs PostgreSQL, and it runs the server in production.
PostgreSQLVersion 16 or later. Docker provides it.

Which path do I choose? To change the code and see it reload, follow Local development. To run the server on a host, follow Production deploy.

03 Database

Database & migrations

The server stores all state in PostgreSQL 16 or later. It applies schema changes with versioned migrations.

How migrations run

The migration files live in internal/store/migrations. Each change has an up file and a down file. The server applies pending migrations on start when AUTO_MIGRATE=true. To run them by hand, use the make targets.

The make targets read DATABASE_URL. Load your .env first with set -a; source .env; set +a, or the targets use the local default.

Schema conventions

  • Every table uses a UUID v7 primary key. These keys sort by time.
  • Every timestamp is TIMESTAMPTZ in UTC.
  • A soft delete sets deleted_at; it does not remove the row.
  • Every migration has an up file and a down file.
  • Migration files use the name NNNN_description.up.sql and .down.sql.

Core tables

TablePurpose
usersThe canonical user record.
user_credentialsPasswords (argon2id hash) and passkeys.
user_mfa_methodsTOTP secrets and WebAuthn credentials.
sessionsBrowser sessions with a sliding expiry.
clientsRegistered OIDC/OAuth applications.
authorization_codesShort-lived OAuth authorization codes.
access_tokensIssued access tokens.
refresh_tokensIssued refresh tokens.
cas_servicesRegistered CAS service URLs.
upstream_providersFederated IdP configuration.
audit_logThe immutable, append-only event log.

Reset the database

To delete all local data, remove the Docker volume. Then start again from the development steps.

04 Scripts & tests

Make targets & tests

The Makefile drives every task. Run make help to list all targets.

Build & run

make buildCompiles one binary with the web UI embedded into ./bin/iam-server.
make runBuilds, then runs the binary.
make dev-serverRuns the server with go run for development.

Test

The tests use a real Postgres through testcontainers-go. Docker must be running.

make testRuns all unit and integration tests with the race detector.
make test-coverRuns the tests and reports coverage.
make smoke-testRuns a black-box check against a running server (BASE_URL=http://localhost:8080).

Web UI

make web-devStarts the Vite dev server with hot reload on port 5173.
make web-buildBuilds the React admin UI into web/dist.
make web-lintChecks lint and format with Biome (no writes).
make web-formatFixes lint and format with Biome.

Keys & users

make keygenGenerates an RSA signing key at ./signing.pem (development).
make rotate-key dir=/etc/iam/keysGenerates a new signing key in a keys directory.
make seed-user email=… password=… admin=1Creates a user account.
make grant-admin email=…Promotes an existing user to admin.

Security scans

make vulnScans Go dependencies for known vulnerabilities (govulncheck).
make vuln-webScans the web UI's production dependencies (npm audit, high and up).

06 Contribution

Contribution rules

Follow these rules for every change. They keep the codebase small, safe, and consistent.

The development loop

Set up your machine with the Local development steps. Then use this loop for each change:

  1. Create a branch. Use a prefix: feat/, fix/, chore/, or docs/.
  2. Write the code and a test for it.
  3. Run make test and make lint.
  4. Commit with a Conventional Commit message (for example, feat: add WebAuthn enrollment).
  5. Open a pull request.

Pull request rules

  • The CI must pass.
  • One reviewer must approve.
  • The code must have no lint warnings.

Git conventions

Branchesfeat/, fix/, chore/, docs/
CommitsConventional Commits (type: summary).
ReleasesA semver tag (v1.2.3) triggers the release build.

Add a dependency

Keep the runtime section of go.mod short. Before you add a dependency, answer these questions. If a pull request adds a require entry, justify it in the commit message.

QuestionAction
Is it a protocol or spec implementation? (WebAuthn, JWT, TOTP)Keep it. Specs have sharp edges and a subtle attack surface.
Is it glue or boilerplate? (routing, config, logging)Replace it with a stdlib equivalent.
Is it a dev-time code generator? (sqlc, migrate)Keep it. It has zero runtime cost and prevents bugs.
Would it take under 200 lines to write? (JWKS serialisation)Write it in internal/crypto.
Is it maintained by the Go team? (golang.org/x/*)Treat it as an extended stdlib.

Code style

  • The dependency flow is api → auth → store. It never runs the other way.
  • internal/ packages are private. pkg/ packages are public.
  • Define sentinel errors in each package. Wrap errors with context.
  • HTTP handlers return RFC 7807 Problem JSON on error.
  • Put unit tests next to the source file (foo_test.go).

07 Production deploy

Deploy to production

{{ template "guide" (index .Guides 1) }}

Back up two things

The pgdata volume holds your whole database. The signing/signing.pem file signs your tokens. If you lose the signing key, every issued token stops working. Back up both, off-host.

Check before you go live

  • BASE_URL matches what users type (scheme, host, no trailing slash).
  • <BASE_URL>/.well-known/openid-configuration returns JSON.
  • <BASE_URL>/healthz returns ok.
  • Your admin account has MFA enrolled.

Caddy example

Caddy is the documented companion proxy. It handles TLS for you.

09 CSRF

CSRF protection

CSRF is cross-site request forgery. An attacker tricks a browser into sending a request with the user's session cookie attached. The server blocks this with a double-submit cookie.

How it works

The server issues a random token in a cookie named iam_csrf. The cookie is readable by JavaScript, so the admin UI can echo it. On every state-changing request, the client must present the same token. The server compares the two values.

  • The admin UI sends the token in the X-CSRF-Token header.
  • A server-rendered form sends the token in the _csrf field.

The server checks POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE requests. It does not check GET, HEAD, or OPTIONS, because those requests are safe.

Which routes are checked

The server protects the browser flows:

  • POST /cas/login
  • /password/forgot and POST /password/reset
  • The /mfa/* POST routes (verify and enroll)
  • The /admin/v1/* POST, PATCH, and DELETE routes

Which routes are exempt

Machine-to-machine and read-only routes skip CSRF. A browser does not drive them, so a forged request is not a risk.

/oauth2/tokenA client authenticates with its credentials.
/oauth2/userinfoA bearer token authenticates the request.
/oauth2/introspectA client authenticates with its credentials.
/oauth2/revokeA client authenticates with its credentials.
/federation/The OAuth state parameter provides CSRF protection.
/proxy/verifyRead-only. It changes no state.
/metrics, /healthz, /readyzRead-only operations endpoints.

When you add a new state-changing route, review the exempt list. A route added without review can silently weaken the protection.

Send the token from a client

Read the iam_csrf cookie. Send its value in the X-CSRF-Token header.

10 CAS

CAS

CAS is the Central Authentication Service protocol. The server accepts CAS 2.0 and 3.0. Older apps use it for single sign-on.

The sign-in flow

  1. An app sends the user to /cas/login?service=<app-url>.
  2. The server signs the user in. It issues a service ticket (ST).
  3. The server sends the user back to the app with the ticket.
  4. The app calls a validate endpoint to check the ticket.
  5. The server returns the user and, in CAS 3.0, the released attributes.

Endpoints

GET/cas/loginSigns in and issues a service ticket.
GET/cas/serviceValidateCAS 2.0 ticket validation.
GET/cas/p3/serviceValidateCAS 3.0 ticket validation, with attributes.
GET/cas/logoutEnds the session (single logout).

The CAS-to-SSO bridge

A CAS app can use a modern provider. When the user has no local session, the server starts an upstream OIDC or OAuth flow (Google, GitHub, and others). It maps the returned identity to a local user. Then it issues the CAS ticket.

Client App  --CAS login-->  IAM Server  --OIDC flow-->  Google / GitHub
                <-- ST --                   <-- id_token --
Client App  --validate ST--> IAM Server
                <-- user attrs --

Register a CAS service

The server issues a ticket only for a registered service URL. Add the service in the admin UI, or with the admin API.

To limit a service to some users, turn on require_allowlist for that service. Then add the allowed emails. The server checks the list at ticket issuance.

11 OpenID Connect

OpenID Connect & OAuth 2.0

The server is a standards-conformant authorization server. Modern apps use it for sign-in and for API authorization.

Supported flows

  • Authorization Code with PKCE: for web apps, single-page apps, and mobile apps.
  • Client Credentials: for machine-to-machine access.
  • Refresh Token: to get a new access token without a new sign-in.

The Implicit flow and the Password flow are off by default.

Discovery

An app reads the server's metadata from the discovery document. It finds every endpoint and the signing keys there.

The Authorization Code flow with PKCE

  1. The app creates a code_verifier and a code_challenge.
  2. The app sends the user to /oauth2/authorize with the challenge.
  3. The user signs in and grants consent.
  4. The server returns an authorization code to the app.
  5. The app calls /oauth2/token with the code and the verifier.
  6. The server returns an id_token and an access_token.

PKCE is mandatory for public clients. The server accepts the S256 method only.

Register a client

Add a client in the admin UI, or with the admin API. Set the redirect URIs and the scopes. A public client (a single-page app or a mobile app) uses PKCE and holds no secret.

Exchange a code for tokens

12 MFA

Multi-factor authentication

MFA adds a second factor to sign-in. The server challenges the user after the password step.

Methods

MethodNotes
TOTPA 6-digit code from an authenticator app (RFC 6238). Enroll with a QR code.
WebAuthn / passkeyA FIDO2 security key or a platform passkey. Supports passwordless sign-in.
Backup codesTen single-use codes. Use one when you lose your other factor.

Enroll a factor

A signed-in user enrolls a factor at /mfa/enroll.

  1. Open /mfa/enroll.
  2. For TOTP, scan the QR code. Enter the 6-digit code to confirm.
  3. For a passkey, follow the browser prompt.
  4. Generate backup codes. Store them in a safe place.

Enforce MFA

You control MFA at two levels:

  • Per user: a user enrolls a factor. The server then challenges that user.
  • Per client: a client sends acr_values to require MFA for its sign-in.
  • Global: set FORCE_MFA=true to require MFA for everyone.

Enroll a second factor on your admin account right after the first sign-in. Generate backup codes at the same time.

13 Federation

Set up federation (upstream SSO)

Federation lets users sign in with an external provider. The server maps the external identity to a local user.

How linking works

On the provider callback, the server does three checks in order:

  1. It looks for a user already linked to this provider and subject. If it finds one, it signs the user in.
  2. It looks for a user with the same email. If it finds one, it prompts the user to link the accounts.
  3. If it finds neither, it creates a new user and links the provider.

Set up Google

  1. Create an OAuth client in the Google Cloud console.
  2. Set the redirect URI to <BASE_URL>/oauth/callback/google.
  3. Set GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID and GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET.
  4. Restart the server. A Google button appears on the sign-in page.

Set up GitHub

  1. Create an OAuth app in GitHub settings.
  2. Set the callback URL to <BASE_URL>/oauth/callback/github.
  3. Set GITHUB_CLIENT_ID and GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET.
  4. Restart the server. A GitHub button appears on the sign-in page.

Set up any OIDC provider

Use the generic OIDC connector for Microsoft, Okta, GitLab, Keycloak, and others. List each provider by a slug. Then add its four variables.

Set the redirect URI at the provider to <BASE_URL>/oauth/callback/<slug>. For the example above, the slugs are microsoft and okta.

In Docker Compose, the variables must reach the container. Add each variable to the iam.environment block, or the provider stays inactive.

15 Security

Security defaults

The server ships with safe defaults. This section lists them so you know what protects your deployment.

Passwords & sessions

  • The server hashes passwords with Argon2id.
  • Session cookies are HMAC-SHA256 signed. They set HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite=Lax.
  • A https BASE_URL turns on the Secure flag automatically.

Response headers

The server sets these headers on every response:

Content-Security-PolicyRestricts sources to same-origin. It blocks external requests.
Strict-Transport-SecurityPins HTTPS for one year (only when BASE_URL is https).
X-Frame-Options: DENYBlocks embedding in an iframe (anti-clickjacking).
X-Content-Type-OptionsBlocks MIME-type sniffing.
Referrer-PolicySends the origin only across sites, not the full URL.
Permissions-PolicyDisables APIs the server does not use.

Rate limits

  • The login endpoint accepts 5 requests per minute per IP.
  • The token endpoint accepts 20 requests per minute per client.

Report a vulnerability

Do not open a public issue for a security problem. Report it privately. See SECURITY.md in the repository.

16 Operations

Operations

Run and maintain the server after it is live.

Health endpoints

GET/healthzLiveness. Returns 200 whenever the process is up.
GET/readyzReadiness. Returns 200 only when the database is reachable.
GET/metricsPrometheus metrics.

Rotate the signing key

Rotate the key with no downtime. Old tokens stay valid until they expire.

  1. Generate a new key. Add it to the JWKS as a second key.
  2. Deploy. The server signs new tokens with the new key. It verifies old tokens against both keys.
  3. Wait for the maximum token lifetime to pass.
  4. Remove the old key from the JWKS.
